paragraphs.context: All children, except one, grow up. They soon know that they will grow up
paragraphs.mainIdea: Wendy learns when she is two that she must grow up. Her mother wishes she could stay small forever.
paragraphs.simple: All children grow up, except one. Children soon know that they will grow up. Wendy learned it in this way. One day, when she was two years old, she was playing in a garden. She pulled off another flower and ran with it to her mother. I think she must have looked very lovely, because Mrs. Darling put her hand to her heart and cried, "Oh, why can't you stay like this forever!" That was all they said about it. But from then on Wendy knew that she must grow up. You always know after you are two. Two is the beginning of the end.

paragraphs.context: Mrs. Darling first heard of Peter when she was tidying up her children’s minds
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Darling hears of Peter when she tidies her children's minds. The writer says every good mother does this at night.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Darling first heard of Peter when she was tidying up her children's minds. Every good mother does this each night after her children are asleep. She looks through their minds and puts things straight for the next morning. She puts back in the right places the many things that moved about during the day. If you could stay awake (but of course you can't), you would see your own mother doing this. It is very interesting to watch. It is like tidying drawers. You would see her on her knees, staying a while in a playful way over some of your things, and wondering where you found this thing. Some things she finds are sweet and some are not so sweet. She presses this one to her cheek as if it were as nice as a kitten, and quickly puts that one out of sight. When you wake in the morning, the naughty things and bad feelings that you took to bed have been folded up small and put at the bottom of your mind. On top, nicely aired, are your prettier thoughts, ready for you to put on.

paragraphs.context: Alas, he would not listen. He was determined to show who was master
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Darling will not listen to his wife. He drags Nana out of the nursery and ties her up, and he feels ashamed.
paragraphs.simple: Sadly, he would not listen. He had decided to show who was master in that house. Orders did not bring Nana out of her kennel, so he pulled her out with sweet words. Then he took hold of her roughly and dragged her from the nursery. He felt ashamed of himself, and yet he did it. It was all because his nature was too loving and wanted people to admire him very much. After he tied her up in the backyard, the unhappy father went and sat in the passage with his knuckles to his eyes.

paragraphs.context: Stars are beautiful, but they may not take an active part in anything
paragraphs.mainIdea: The stars may only look on, as a punishment. Tonight the little stars are on Peter's side and want the grown-ups out of the way.
paragraphs.simple: No. 27 was only a few yards away. A little snow had fallen, so Father and Mother Darling stepped carefully over it, to keep their shoes clean. They were the only people in the street, and all the stars were watching them. Stars are beautiful, but they cannot take an active part in anything. They must just look on forever. It is a punishment for something they did so long ago that no star now knows what it was. So the older stars have glassy eyes and seldom speak (winking is the star language), but the little ones still wonder. They are not really friendly to Peter, who has a naughty way of creeping up behind them and trying to blow them out. But they love fun so much that tonight they were on his side, and wanted the grown-ups out of the way. So when the door of 27 closed on Mr. and Mrs. Darling, there was a great noise and excitement in the sky, and the smallest of all the stars in the Milky Way screamed out:

paragraphs.context: He tried to stick it on with soap from the bathroom
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter cannot join his shadow back on to himself. He is shocked, sits on the floor and cries.
paragraphs.simple: If Peter thought at all (but I do not think he ever thought), he thought that his shadow and he would join like drops of water when they were brought near each other. When they did not join, he was shocked. He tried to stick the shadow on with soap from the bathroom, but that did not work either. A sudden shake went through Peter, and he sat on the floor and cried.

paragraphs.context: talking about what I was to be when I became a man
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter tells Wendy why he ran away. He does not want to be a man. He wants to be a little boy and have fun always.
paragraphs.simple: Peter explained in a low voice that it was because he heard his father and mother talking about what he would be when he became a man. He was now very upset. "I never want to be a man," he said strongly. "I always want to be a little boy and have fun. So I ran away to Kensington Gardens and lived a very long time with the fairies."

paragraphs.context: when the first baby laughed for the first time, its laugh broke into a thousand pieces
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter tells Wendy how fairies began. They began with a baby's first laugh.
paragraphs.simple: You see, Wendy, when the first baby laughed for the first time, its laugh broke into a thousand pieces. All the pieces went skipping about. That was the beginning of fairies.

paragraphs.context: His way was to pursue birds who had food in their mouths
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children fly for days. Peter gets food for them in an odd way, by taking it from birds.
paragraphs.simple: Sometimes it was dark and sometimes light. Now they were very cold, and then too warm. Did they really feel hungry at times, or were they only pretending, because Peter had such a jolly new way of feeding them? His way was to chase birds that had food in their mouths that humans could eat, and take it from them. Then the birds would follow and take it back. They would all chase each other happily for miles, and at last they would part, each saying kind things to the other. But Wendy saw, with gentle worry, that Peter did not seem to know that this was a rather odd way of getting your bread and butter. He did not even know that there are other ways.

paragraphs.context: Tink was not all bad: or, rather, she was all bad just now
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tink is full of jealousy of Wendy. Fairies can only feel one thing at a time. Tink is not all bad.
paragraphs.simple: Tink was not all bad. Or rather, she was all bad just now, but sometimes she was all good. Fairies have to be one thing or the other, because they are so small that they have room for only one feeling at a time. They are allowed to change, but it must be a complete change. At present she was full of jealousy of Wendy. Wendy could not understand what she said in her lovely tinkle. I think some of it was bad words, but it sounded kind, and Tink flew back and forward, plainly meaning "Follow me, and all will be well."

paragraphs.context: The first to pass is Tootles, not the least brave but the most unfortunate
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tootles is brave but unlucky. He always misses the big adventures. Tink thinks he is the easiest boy to trick.
paragraphs.simple: The first to pass is Tootles. He is not the least brave of that bold group, but he is the most unlucky. He had been in fewer adventures than any of them. The big things always happened just when he had stepped round the corner. All would be quiet, he would go off to gather a few sticks for firewood, and when he came back the others would be sweeping up the blood. This bad luck gave a gentle sadness to his face. But it did not make him sour. It made him sweeter, so that he was the most humble of the boys. Poor kind Tootles, there is danger in the air for you tonight. Take care that an adventure is not offered to you which, if you accept it, will bring you deep sorrow. Tootles, the fairy Tink is looking for a tool because she wants to make trouble this night, and she thinks you are the easiest of the boys to trick. Beware of Tinker Bell.

paragraphs.context: To return to the ship,” Hook replied slowly through his teeth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hook plans to make a big, rich cake and leave it by the lagoon. He thinks the boys will eat it and die.
paragraphs.simple: "We will go back to the ship," Hook said slowly through his teeth, "and cook a large rich cake, a jolly thick one, with green sugar on it. There can be only one room below, because there is only one chimney. The silly moles did not have the sense to see that they did not need a door each. That shows they have no mother. We will leave the cake on the shore of the mermaids' lagoon. These boys are always swimming there, playing with the mermaids. They will find the cake and eat it up fast, because, having no mother, they do not know how dangerous it is to eat rich damp cake." He burst into laughter, not hollow laughter now, but honest laughter. "Aha, they will die."

paragraphs.context: The difference between him and the other boys at such a time
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter cannot tell make-believe from real things. The other boys can, and this sometimes troubles them.
paragraphs.simple: The difference between Peter and the other boys at such a time was that they knew it was make-believe. To Peter, make-believe and true were exactly the same thing. This sometimes troubled them, as when they had to pretend that they had had their dinners.

paragraphs.context: It certainly does need a chimney,” said John importantly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter finds a chimney for Wendy's house in John's hat. Smoke comes out of it at once.
paragraphs.simple: "It certainly does need a chimney," said John importantly. This gave Peter an idea. He took the hat off John's head, knocked out the bottom, and put the hat on the roof. The little house was so pleased to have such a good chimney that smoke came out of the hat at once, as if to say thank you.

paragraphs.context: One of the first things Peter did next day was to measure Wendy and John and Michael
paragraphs.mainIdea: Each boy needs a hollow tree that fits him. Going up and down is easy only if the tree fits.
paragraphs.simple: One of the first things Peter did next day was to measure Wendy and John and Michael for hollow trees. Hook, you remember, had laughed at the boys for thinking they needed a tree each. But he did not know. Unless your tree fitted you, it was hard to go up and down, and no two of the boys were quite the same size. When you fitted, you drew in your breath at the top, and down you went at just the right speed. To go up, you drew in and let out your breath one after the other, and so wriggled up. When you have learned how, you can do these things without thinking about them, and then nothing can be more graceful.

paragraphs.context: Adventures, of course, as we shall see, were of daily occurrence
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter invents a game of pretending not to have adventures. He likes it for a while and then loses interest.
paragraphs.simple: Adventures happened every day, as we shall see. But at this time Peter invented, with Wendy's help, a new game that he liked very much, until he suddenly lost all interest in it. As you have been told, this always happened with his games. The game was to pretend not to have adventures. It meant doing what John and Michael had done all their lives: sitting on stools and throwing balls in the air, pushing each other, going out for walks and coming back without having killed even a grizzly. It was a great sight to see Peter doing nothing on a stool. He could not help looking serious at such times, because sitting still seemed to him such a funny thing to do. He said proudly that he had gone for a walk for the good of his health. For several suns these were the newest of all adventures to him. John and Michael had to pretend to be happy about it too, or he would have been hard on them.

paragraphs.context: If you shut your eyes and are a lucky one, you may see at times
paragraphs.mainIdea: If you shut your eyes, you may see colours that become the lagoon. It is as near as you get to it on the mainland.
paragraphs.simple: If you shut your eyes and are lucky, you may sometimes see a shapeless pool of lovely pale colours in the dark. Then if you squeeze your eyes tighter, the pool starts to take shape. The colours become so bright that, with one more squeeze, they must catch fire. But just before they catch fire, you see the lagoon. This is the nearest you ever get to it on the mainland: just one heavenly moment. If there could be two moments, you might see the surf and hear the mermaids singing.

paragraphs.context: Not the pain of this but its unfairness was what dazed Peter
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hook's bite shocks Peter because it is unfair. The writer says Peter is different because he always forgets unfairness.
paragraphs.simple: It was not the pain of the bite but the unfairness of it that shocked Peter. It made him helpless. He could only stare, filled with horror. Every child feels this way the first time someone is unfair to him. All he thinks he has a right to, when he comes to you to be yours, is fairness. After you have been unfair to him he will love you again, but he will never afterwards be quite the same boy. No one ever gets over the first unfairness. No one except Peter. He often met it, but he always forgot it. I think that was the real difference between him and all the rest.

paragraphs.context: It was not really a piece of paper; it was the Never bird
paragraphs.mainIdea: The thing on the water is the Never bird. She is trying to reach Peter in her nest to save him.
paragraphs.simple: It was not really a piece of paper. It was the Never bird, making great efforts to reach Peter on her nest. By working her wings, in a way she had learned since the nest fell into the water, she could guide her strange boat to some extent. But by the time Peter knew who it was, she was very tired. She had come to save him. She had come to give him her nest, even though there were eggs in it. I rather wonder at the bird, because he had been nice to her, but he had also sometimes made her suffer. I can only think that, like Mrs. Darling and the rest of them, she was touched because he had all his first teeth.

paragraphs.context: The Never bird saw at once what he was up to
paragraphs.mainIdea: The bird sees Peter's plan and screams that she likes it. Peter sails away in the nest, and the bird sits on her eggs in the hat.
paragraphs.simple: The Never bird saw at once what he was doing, and she screamed that she admired him. Sadly, Peter crowed that he agreed with her. Then he got into the nest, set the stave up in it as a mast, and hung up his shirt as a sail. At the same moment the bird flew down onto the hat and again sat comfortably on her eggs. She drifted one way and he was carried the other way, and both were cheering.

paragraphs.context: We have now reached the evening that was to be known among them as the Night of Nights
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the evening of the Night of Nights. The boys eat their meal, and Peter has gone out to find the time.
paragraphs.simple: We have now reached the evening that was to be called the Night of Nights, because of its adventures and what came of them. The day had been almost quiet, as if it was quietly gathering its forces. Now the redskins in their blankets were at their posts above, and below the children were having their evening meal. Only Peter was missing. He had gone out to get the time. On the island, the way to get the time was to find the crocodile and stay near him until the clock struck.

paragraphs.context: None of them knew. Perhaps it was best not to know
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children have one last happy hour. They sing, dance and have a pillow fight before the story.
paragraphs.simple: None of them knew. Maybe it was best not to know. Not knowing gave them one more happy hour. As it was to be their last hour on the island, let us be glad that there were sixty happy minutes in it. They sang and danced in their nightgowns. It was a deliciously creepy song, in which they pretended to be frightened of their own shadows. They hardly knew that soon shadows would close in on them, and they would shrink from them in real fear. The dance was so noisy and happy, and how they pushed and hit each other on the bed and off it! It was more a pillow fight than a dance. When it was finished, the pillows asked for one more round, like partners who know that they may never meet again. And the stories they told, before it was time for Wendy's good night story! Even Slightly tried to tell a story that night, but the beginning was so very dull that it shocked even him, and he said sadly:

paragraphs.context: But of course he cared very much; and he was so full of wrath against grownups
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter is angry with grown-ups. He breathes fast because of a saying in the Neverland that each breath kills a grown-up.
paragraphs.simple: But of course he cared very much. He was so full of anger against grown-ups, who, as usual, were spoiling everything, that as soon as he got inside his tree he breathed short quick breaths on purpose, about five to a second. He did this because there is a saying in the Neverland that every time you breathe, a grown-up dies. And Peter was killing them off as fast as he could, as a way to hurt them back.

paragraphs.context: That was the story, and they were as pleased with it as the fair narrator herself
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer says children go off without a care, and come back when they need help, sure that their mothers will hug them.
paragraphs.simple: That was the story, and they were as pleased with it as the fair story-teller herself. Everything was just as it should be, you see. Off we skip like the most heartless things in the world, which is what children are, but so attractive. We have a completely selfish time. Then when we need special care, we nobly come back for it, sure that we shall be hugged and not smacked.

paragraphs.context: Peter was such a small boy that one tends to wonder at the man’s hatred of him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hook hates Peter very much, more than the crocodile story explains. The writer says the reason is Peter's cockiness.
paragraphs.simple: Peter was such a small boy that one wonders at the man's hatred of him. It is true that he had thrown Hook's arm to the crocodile. But even this, and the greater danger to Hook's life that came from the crocodile not giving up, hardly explain such a hatred that would not stop and wished harm. The truth is that there was something about Peter that pushed the pirate captain to wild anger. It was not his courage. It was not his pleasant looks. It was not --. There is no use going round the subject, because we know well what it was, and we have to tell it. It was Peter's cockiness.

paragraphs.context: The doomed children answered with a cheer that was music to the black hearts above
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys cheer and say goodbye to Peter again. The pirates are glad that the boys will come up the trees.
paragraphs.simple: The children, who were doomed, answered with a cheer. It was music to the black hearts above. Almost at once they said their goodbyes to Peter again. This puzzled the pirates, but all their other feelings were swallowed by a low delight that the enemy were about to come up the trees. They smirked at each other and rubbed their hands. Quickly and silently, Hook gave his orders: one man to each tree, and the others to stand in a line two yards apart.

paragraphs.context: Unaware of the tragedy being enacted above, Peter had continued
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter tries to show that he does not care that Wendy has gone. He plays his pipes and then falls asleep in the middle of a laugh.
paragraphs.simple: Peter did not know about the sad things that were happening above. For a little time after the children left, he had gone on playing happily on his pipes. This was no doubt a rather sad try to show himself that he did not care. Then he decided not to take his medicine, to make Wendy sad. Then he lay down on the bed outside the cover, to annoy her even more, because she had always tucked them inside it, since you never know that you may not grow cold at the turn of the night. Then he nearly cried. But it came to him how angry she would be if he laughed instead, so he laughed a proud laugh and fell asleep in the middle of it.

paragraphs.context: The clapping stopped suddenly; as if countless mothers had rushed to their nurseries
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children's clapping saves Tink. She is soon well and lively again.
paragraphs.simple: The clapping stopped suddenly, as if countless mothers had rushed to their nurseries to see what on earth was happening. But already Tink was saved. First her voice grew strong. Then she popped out of bed. Then she was flashing through the room, more merry and rude than ever. She never thought of thanking those who believed, but she would have liked to get at the ones who had hissed.

paragraphs.context: Hook was not his true name. To reveal who he really was would even at this date
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hook is not his real name. He went to a famous school, and its ways stay with him, above all the wish for good form.
paragraphs.simple: Hook was not his true name. To tell who he really was would, even at this date, set the country in a blaze. But as those who read between the lines must already have guessed, he had been at a famous public school. Its ways still stayed with him like clothes, which are largely what they are about. So even now he disliked to go on board a ship in the same clothes in which he had fought her. And in his walk he still kept to the school's special slouch. But above all he kept the passion for good form.

paragraphs.context: It is sad to know that not a boy was looking at her as Smee tied her to the mast
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys stare at the plank and cannot think. None of them looks at Wendy.
paragraphs.simple: It is sad to know that not a boy was looking at her as Smee tied her to the mast. All their eyes were on the plank, the last little walk they were about to take. They could no longer hope that they would walk it bravely, because they were not able to think any more. They could only stare and shake.

paragraphs.context: Odd things happen to all of us on our way through life without our noticing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter sees that the crocodile is no longer ticking. He decides that the clock has run down.
paragraphs.simple: Odd things happen to all of us on our way through life, and for a time we do not notice that they have happened. For example, we suddenly find that we have been deaf in one ear for we don't know how long, but say half an hour. Now such a thing had happened that night to Peter. When we last saw him, he was creeping across the island with one finger on his lips and his dagger ready. He had seen the crocodile go past without noticing anything strange about it. But after a while he remembered that it had not been ticking. At first he thought this was strange and frightening, but soon he rightly decided that the clock had run down.

paragraphs.context: He had one last triumph, which I think we need not grudge him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hook wins one last thing. Peter kicks him instead of stabbing him,.
paragraphs.simple: He had one last win, which I think we need not refuse him. He stood on the bulwark and looked back over his shoulder at Peter flying through the air. With a movement, he asked Peter to use his foot. It made Peter kick instead of stab.

paragraphs.context: The only change to be seen in the night-nursery is that between nine and six
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Darling thinks everything is his fault. He crawls into the kennel.
paragraphs.simple: The only change to be seen in the night-nursery is that between nine and six the kennel is no longer there. When the children flew away, Mr. Darling felt deep inside that all the blame was his, for having chained Nana up, and that from first to last she had been wiser than he. Of course, as we have seen, he was quite a simple man. He might have passed for a boy again if he had been able to take off his baldness. But he also had a noble sense of fairness and the courage of a lion to do what seemed right to him. After thinking the matter over with great care after the children's flight, he went down on his hands and knees and crawled into the kennel. Mrs. Darling asked him kindly many times to come out, but he answered sadly and firmly:

paragraphs.context: And so when Mrs. Darling went back to the night-nursery to see if her husband was asleep
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Darling finds the children in their beds. She thinks it is a dream.
paragraphs.simple: And so when Mrs. Darling went back to the night-nursery to see if her husband was asleep, all the beds were full. The children waited for her cry of joy, but it did not come. She saw them, but she did not believe they were there. You see, she saw them in their beds so often in her dreams that she thought this was just the dream still hanging around her.

paragraphs.context: That was the last time the girl Wendy ever saw him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Wendy never sees Peter again as a girl. She grows up and marries, and the writer says she wanted to grow up.
paragraphs.simple: That was the last time the girl Wendy ever saw him. For a little longer she tried, for his sake, not to have growing pains. She felt she was not loyal to him when she got a prize for general knowledge. But the years came and went without bringing the careless boy. When they met again, Wendy was a married woman, and Peter was no more to her than a little dust in the box in which she had kept her toys. Wendy was grown up. You need not be sorry for her. She was one of the kind that likes to grow up. In the end she grew up of her own free will a day quicker than other girls.

paragraphs.context: As you look at Wendy you may see her hair becoming white
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter keeps coming for the daughters of Wendy's family. The story will go on as long as children are gay and innocent and heartless.
paragraphs.simple: As you look at Wendy, you may see her hair becoming white and her figure becoming small again, because all this happened long ago. Jane is now an ordinary grown-up, with a daughter called Margaret. Every spring-cleaning time, except when he forgets, Peter comes for Margaret and takes her to the Neverland. There she tells him stories about himself, and he listens eagerly. When Margaret grows up she will have a daughter, who is to be Peter's mother in turn. And so it will go on, as long as children are gay and innocent and heartless.

paragraphs.context: Avast belay, yo ho, heave to, A-pirating we go
paragraphs.mainIdea: The pirates sing a short song as they come through the wood.
paragraphs.simple: This is the pirates' song. They shout old orders from a ship, then say they are going out to steal. If a shot parts them, they will meet again under the sea.

paragraphs.context: Yo ho, yo ho, the pirate life, The flag o’ skull and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The boys hear another pirate song, about the flag and the rope.
paragraphs.simple: The song says the pirate life is merry. It names the flag with a skull and bones, a happy hour, a rope of hemp, and the bottom of the sea.

paragraphs.context: I wish I had a pretty house, The littlest ever seen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Wendy sings in her sleep for a very small house.
paragraphs.simple: Wendy sings that she wants the smallest pretty house, with funny little red walls and a roof of green moss.

paragraphs.context: Yo ho, yo ho, the frisky plank, You walks along it so
paragraphs.mainIdea: Hook sings a pirate song about walking the plank.
paragraphs.simple: Hook sings that the plank is lively. You walk along it, it tips down, and you fall to the bottom of the sea.

paragraphs.context: dropped an acorn button into her hand; so she
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peter does not know what a kiss is, so he gives Wendy an acorn button.
paragraphs.simple: Peter asks if he may give Wendy a kiss. She holds up her face. He does not kiss her. He drops a button made from an acorn into her hand. She says she will wear his kiss on a chain. Later that button saves her life.

paragraphs.context: instantly, “there are birds called Wendies
paragraphs.mainIdea: Slightly thinks a Wendy is a kind of bird.
paragraphs.simple: Slightly says he remembers birds that are called Wendies. He thinks the girl in the sky is one of those birds.

sentences.context: If you could keep awake (but of course you can’t) you would see your own mother doing this
sentences.simple: If you could stay awake, you would see your own mother doing this. But of course you cannot stay awake.
sentences.grammar: 'If you could ... you would ...' talks about something that is not real, and the writer says in brackets that you cannot do it.

sentences.context: the many gentlemen who had been boys when she was a girl
sentences.simple: This is how Mr. Darling won her. Many men had been boys when she was a girl. They all found out at the same time that they loved her. They all ran to her house to ask her to marry them, except Mr. Darling, who took a cab and got there first. So he got her.
sentences.grammar: 'The way ... was this:' uses a colon to start the story; 'had been boys' is the past perfect for a time before she was a girl.

sentences.context: On these magic shores children at play are forever beaching their coracles
sentences.simple: On these magic shores, children who are playing are always pulling their little boats onto the beach.
sentences.grammar: 'are forever + -ing' (present continuous with 'forever') shows something that happens again and again.

sentences.context: she had believed in him at the time, but now that she was married
sentences.simple: She had believed in him at that time, but now she was married and full of sense, and she quite doubted that there was any such person.
sentences.grammar: 'had believed' (past perfect) is an earlier time than 'now'; 'now that' means 'because now'.

sentences.context: If only I had not accepted that invitation to dine at 27
sentences.simple: I wish I had not said yes to the invitation to have dinner at 27.
sentences.grammar: 'If only + had + past participle' is a wish about the past: it happened and she is sorry.

sentences.context: They sat thus night after night recalling that fatal Friday
sentences.simple: They sat like this night after night and remembered that terrible Friday, until every small thing about it was pressed into their minds. It showed through on the other side, like the faces on bad coins.
sentences.grammar: 'recalling' (-ing) tells what they were doing while they sat; 'till' means 'until'; 'like the faces on a bad coinage' is a comparison.

sentences.context: Some men would have resented her being able to do it so easily
sentences.simple: Some men would have been angry that she could do it so easily.
sentences.grammar: 'would have resented' says what some men would have felt; 'her being able to' means 'that she was able to'.

sentences.context: an example to you, Michael, if I hadn’t lost the bottle
sentences.simple: I would take it now as an example to you, Michael, if I had not lost the bottle.
sentences.grammar: 'I would take it ... if I hadn't lost' is an unreal condition: he says he would do it now, but he says he cannot because the bottle is lost.

sentences.context: had it not been that the little stars were watching them
sentences.simple: They would have reached the nursery in time if the little stars had not been watching them.
sentences.grammar: 'Had it not been that...' means 'If it had not been that...'. The word order is turned round to talk about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: such a home life that to know fairies struck her as quite delightful
sentences.simple: Wendy had lived such a home life that knowing fairies seemed very lovely to her.
sentences.grammar: 'such a ... that ...' shows a result; 'to know fairies' is the subject of the verb 'struck'.

sentences.context: no one can fly unless the fairy dust has been blown on him
sentences.simple: No one can fly unless someone has blown the fairy dust on him.
sentences.grammar: 'unless' means 'if not'; 'has been blown' is the present perfect passive, so the person who blows the dust is not named.

sentences.context: if she would only stand still and let me see her
sentences.simple: I wish she would just stand still and let me see her!
sentences.grammar: 'If ... would only' is a strong wish; 'let me see her' is 'let + object + base verb'.

sentences.context: talking about what I was to be when I became a man
sentences.simple: He heard them talking about what he would be when he became a man.
sentences.grammar: 'what I was to be' means 'what I would be'; 'was to + verb' talks about the future from a time in the past.

sentences.context: when what you want to be asked is Kings of England
sentences.simple: It was like an exam paper that asks about grammar when you want it to ask about the Kings of England.
sentences.grammar: 'what you want to be asked' is a clause that works as the subject of 'is'; 'to be asked' is passive.

sentences.context: more they tried to avoid it, the more certainly did they bump
sentences.simple: They tried to keep away from a cloud in front of them, but the harder they tried, the more surely they hit it.
sentences.grammar: 'The more..., the more...' means that as one thing grows, the other grows too; 'did they bump' puts the verb before the subject.

sentences.context: would have been well for Wendy if at that moment she had dropped the hat
sentences.simple: It would have been good for Wendy if she had dropped the hat at that moment.
sentences.grammar: 'would have been ... if she had dropped' is an unreal past: she did not drop the hat.

sentences.context: if the worst came to the worst, all they had to do
sentences.simple: John said that if things went as badly as they could, all they had to do was fly straight on. The world was round, and in time they must come back to their own window.
sentences.grammar: 'if the worst came to the worst' is a fixed phrase for 'if things go as badly as they can'; 'said that ... was round' is reported speech.

sentences.context: have I not told you that anon fear fell upon them
sentences.simple: Have I not told you that soon fear came over them?
sentences.grammar: 'Have I not told you...?' is a question that needs no answer; the writer reminds the reader. 'Anon' is an old word for 'soon'.

sentences.context: which, if accepted, will plunge you in deepest woe
sentences.simple: Take care that an adventure is not offered to you, because if you accept it, it will bring you deep sorrow.
sentences.grammar: 'if accepted' is short for 'if it is accepted'; 'lest' earlier in the sentence means 'in case'.

sentences.context: Would that he could hear us, but we are not really on the island
sentences.simple: I wish he could hear us, but we are not really on the island.
sentences.grammar: 'Would that...' is an old way to say 'I wish that...'; 'could' shows a wish that is not real.

sentences.context: I have seen a wonderfuller thing
sentences.simple: I have seen something more wonderful.
sentences.grammar: 'Wonderfuller' adds -er to a long adjective, which is a child's way to make a comparative; the usual form is 'more wonderful'.

sentences.context: such a tiny sound that a leaf might have fallen on it and smothered it
sentences.simple: At first it was such a tiny sound that a leaf could have fallen on it and covered it.
sentences.grammar: 'such a ... that ...' shows a result; 'might have fallen' says it was possible, which shows how small the sound was.

sentences.context: Any of the other boys obstructing the fairy path at night they would have mischiefed
sentences.simple: If any of the other boys had stood in the fairy path at night, the fairies would have done them harm. But they only gave Peter's nose a little pull and passed on.
sentences.grammar: 'Any of the other boys...' is put first for effect; the normal order is 'they would have mischiefed any of the other boys'. 'would have + -ed' says what would have happened but did not.

sentences.context: they knew it was make-believe, while to him make-believe and true
sentences.simple: The other boys knew it was make-believe, but for Peter make-believe and true were the same thing.
sentences.grammar: 'while' joins two different ideas: what the boys knew and how Peter felt.

sentences.context: If Wendy’s heart had been beating they would all have heard it
sentences.simple: If Wendy's heart had been beating, they would all have heard it.
sentences.grammar: 'If ... had been beating, ... would have heard' is an unreal past: it talks about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: while you have to be made to fit the tree
sentences.simple: Peter measures you for your tree as carefully as for a suit of clothes. The only difference is that clothes are made to fit you, but you have to be made to fit the tree.
sentences.grammar: 'the only difference being that...' gives the difference after a colon; 'are made to fit' and 'have to be made to fit' are passive.

sentences.context: As time wore on did she think much about the beloved parents
sentences.simple: As time passed, did she think much about the dear parents she had left behind?
sentences.grammar: 'As time wore on' is a time clause that means 'as time passed slowly'; 'she had left' is the past perfect for an earlier time.

sentences.context: he could not stodge just to feel stodgy
sentences.simple: He could really eat if it was part of a game, but he could not stuff himself with heavy food just to feel stuffed.
sentences.grammar: 'just to feel stodgy' (to + verb) gives the reason; 'stodge' is a verb and 'stodgy' is an adjective from the same word.

sentences.context: Had it been so with Peter at that moment I would admit it
sentences.simple: If it had been so with Peter at that moment, I would admit it.
sentences.grammar: 'Had it been so...' means 'If it had been so...'. The word order is turned round to talk about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: Not the pain of this but its unfairness was what dazed Peter
sentences.simple: It was not the pain of the bite that shocked Peter, but the unfairness of it.
sentences.grammar: 'Not the pain ... but its unfairness' is put first to stress it; 'what dazed Peter' is a noun clause after 'was'.

sentences.context: She was to be left on the rock to perish
sentences.simple: The plan was to leave her on the rock to die.
sentences.grammar: 'was to be left' (was to + passive) says what was planned for the future, seen from a time in the past.

sentences.context: Peter may have been about to crow, but his face puckered in a whistle
sentences.simple: Perhaps Peter was just going to crow, but his face pulled into a whistle of surprise instead.
sentences.grammar: 'may have been about to crow' is a guess about the past: it was possible that he was just going to crow.

sentences.context: I wish for the moment I could pretend that this was such a story
sentences.simple: I wish I could pretend for a moment that this was such a story.
sentences.grammar: 'I wish ... could pretend' is a wish about something that is not true; 'such a story' points back to 'fanciful stories'.

sentences.context: It was not to receive his thanks, however, that she hung there in the sky
sentences.simple: She did not hang there in the sky to receive his thanks. She did not even hang there to watch him get into the nest. She hung there to see what he did with her eggs.
sentences.grammar: 'It was not to receive his thanks ... that she hung there' is a cleft sentence: it puts the reason first to stress it; the true reason comes in the third part.

sentences.context: As we shall not see her again, it may be worth mentioning here
sentences.simple: We shall not see her again, so it may be good to say here that all Never birds now build their nests in that shape, with a broad brim.
sentences.grammar: 'As' gives the reason; 'it may be worth mentioning' uses 'it' for the real subject, 'that all Never birds now build...'.

sentences.context: If she had known she would not have snapped
sentences.simple: If she had known, she would not have snapped.
sentences.grammar: 'If she had known, she would not have...' is an unreal past: she did not know, and she did snap.

sentences.context: little witting that so soon shadows would close in upon them
sentences.simple: They hardly knew that so soon shadows would close in on them.
sentences.grammar: 'little witting that...' is an old way to say 'hardly knowing that...'; here 'little' means 'hardly at all'.

sentences.context: they must never hit back at meals, but should refer the matter
sentences.simple: There was a fixed rule that they must never hit back at meals. They should take the matter to Wendy.
sentences.grammar: 'must never' and 'should' are modal verbs for rules; 'but' adds what to do instead.

sentences.context: So uproariously gay was the dance, and how they buffeted each other
sentences.simple: The dance was so noisy and happy, and how they pushed and hit each other on the bed and off it!
sentences.grammar: 'So uproariously gay was the dance' puts the adjective first for stress; the normal order is 'The dance was so uproariously gay'.

sentences.context: I had rather he had been a lady
sentences.simple: I would prefer it if he had been a lady.
sentences.grammar: 'I had rather he had been' is an old way to say 'I would prefer it if he had been'; it shows a wish about the past.

sentences.context: If you knew how great is a mother’s love
sentences.simple: If you knew how great a mother's love is, you would have no fear.
sentences.grammar: 'how great is a mother's love' puts the verb before the subject in an old style; 'If you knew ... you would have' talks about something that is not true now.

sentences.context: Not so much as a sorry-to-lose-you between them
sentences.simple: They did not say even one 'sorry to lose you' to each other!
sentences.grammar: 'Not so much as...' means 'not even'; the sentence has no verb, which shows strong feeling.

sentences.context: he was going to show her, was Peter, that neither did he
sentences.simple: If she did not mind saying goodbye, Peter was going to show her that he did not mind either.
sentences.grammar: 'was Peter' is added to name the person, as in speech; 'neither did he' puts the verb before the subject and means 'he did not mind either'.

sentences.context: They all gathered round him in affright, so alarming was his agitation
sentences.simple: They all gathered round him in fear, because he was so upset that it was frightening.
sentences.grammar: 'so alarming was his agitation' puts 'so + adjective' first, so the verb comes before the subject; the normal order is 'his agitation was so alarming'.

sentences.context: Fain would his dogs have known, as breathing heavily
sentences.simple: His men would gladly have known. They were breathing heavily and wiping their cutlasses. They stood at a safe distance from his hook and looked at this strange man through eyes like a ferret's.
sentences.grammar: 'Fain would his dogs have known' puts 'fain' (gladly) and the verb first, an old style for 'His dogs would gladly have known'.

sentences.context: Had he waited on the rising ground till the proper hour
sentences.simple: If he had waited on the rising ground until the right time, he and his men would probably have been killed.
sentences.grammar: 'Had he waited' means 'If he had waited'; 'would probably have been butchered' says what would likely have happened but did not.

sentences.context: Not all unavenged did they die, for with Lean Wolf fell Alf Mason
sentences.simple: They did not all die without someone getting revenge for them, because Alf Mason fell with Lean Wolf.
sentences.grammar: 'Not all unavenged did they die' puts the first words forward for stress; the normal order is 'They did not all die unavenged'.

sentences.context: had he not been at the tying he would not have discovered
sentences.simple: If he had not been at the tying of the children, he would not have found out Slightly's secret. Without the secret he could not have made his foul try on Peter's life.
sentences.grammar: 'Had he not been' means 'If he had not been'; the word order is turned round to talk about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: Dark as were his thoughts his blue eyes were as soft as the periwinkle
sentences.simple: Although his thoughts were dark, his blue eyes were as soft as the periwinkle.
sentences.grammar: 'Dark as were his thoughts' means 'Although his thoughts were dark'; 'adjective + as + verb + subject' is a formal way to say 'although'.

sentences.context: Lest he should be taken alive, Hook always carried about his person
sentences.simple: Hook always carried a terrible drug on his body, in case he was taken alive.
sentences.grammar: 'Lest he should be taken alive' means 'in case he was taken alive'; 'lest' is a formal word for something you want to avoid.

sentences.context: Had the bo’sun good form without knowing it, which is the best form
sentences.simple: Did the bo'sun have good form without knowing it? That is the best form of all.
sentences.grammar: 'Had the bo'sun good form...?' is an old question style with 'had' as the main verb, in place of 'Did the bo'sun have...'; 'which' points to the whole idea before it.

sentences.context: Fine gentleman though he was, the intensity of his communings had soiled his ruff
sentences.simple: Although he was a fine gentleman, the strength of his deep thoughts had made his ruff dirty.
sentences.grammar: 'Fine gentleman though he was' means 'Although he was a fine gentleman'; 'noun + though + subject + verb' is a formal way to say 'although'.

sentences.context: any other man would have lain with his eyes shut where he fell
sentences.simple: Left so fearfully alone, any other man would have lain where he fell with his eyes shut.
sentences.grammar: 'Left so fearfully alone' is a phrase that gives the reason; 'would have lain' says what another man would have done, but Hook did not.

sentences.context: No sooner did Peter remember it than he heard the ticking
sentences.simple: As soon as Peter remembered it, he heard the ticking.
sentences.grammar: 'No sooner did ... than ...' means 'as soon as'; the helper verb 'did' comes before the subject because 'No sooner' is at the front.

sentences.context: Had the pirates kept together it is certain that they would have won
sentences.simple: If the pirates had kept together, they would certainly have won.
sentences.grammar: 'Had the pirates kept together' means 'If the pirates had kept together'; it talks about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: Misguided man though he was, we may be glad, without sympathising with him
sentences.simple: Although he was a misguided man, we may be glad, without feeling sorry for him, that in the end he was true to the ways of his people.
sentences.grammar: 'Misguided man though he was' means 'Although he was a misguided man'; 'though' comes after the noun.

sentences.context: we purposely stopped the clock that this knowledge might be spared him
sentences.simple: We stopped the clock on purpose so that he would not have this knowledge.
sentences.grammar: 'that ... might be spared him' means 'so that ... would be kept from him'; 'might be spared' is passive.

sentences.context: Would it not serve them jolly well right if they came back
sentences.simple: It would serve them right if they came back and found that their parents were spending the weekend in the country.
sentences.grammar: 'Would it not serve them right if...' is a question with 'not' that expects the answer yes; 'if they came back and found' uses the past for an idea that is not real.

sentences.context: whatever Mr. Darling did he had to do in excess
sentences.simple: Whatever Mr. Darling did, he had to do too much of it, or he soon stopped doing it.
sentences.grammar: 'whatever Mr. Darling did' is a clause that means 'anything that he did'; 'in excess' means 'too much'.

sentences.context: he might have passed for a boy again if he had been able
sentences.simple: He might have been taken for a boy again if he had been able to take off his baldness.
sentences.grammar: 'might have passed ... if he had been able' is an unreal past: he could not take his baldness off, so it did not happen.

sentences.context: Why on earth should their beds be properly aired, seeing that they left them
sentences.simple: Why on earth should their beds be aired well, since they left them in such a hurry and gave no thanks?
sentences.grammar: 'seeing that' means 'because'; 'should' in a 'why' question shows the speaker thinks there is no reason.

sentences.context: he used not to sleep in the kennel
sentences.simple: Did he not use to sleep in the kennel?
sentences.grammar: 'used not to' is an old way to say 'did not use to'; it talks about a habit in the past.

sentences.context: she grew up of her own free will a day quicker than other girls
sentences.simple: In the end she grew up because she wanted to, a day sooner than other girls.
sentences.grammar: 'a day quicker than other girls' is a comparison with 'than'; 'of her own free will' means 'because she chose to'.

sentences.context: Peter did not alight in the church and forbid the banns
sentences.simple: It is strange to think that Peter did not land in the church and say that the wedding must not go on.
sentences.grammar: 'It is strange to think that...' uses 'it' for the real subject, the 'that' clause; 'forbid the banns' means to say that the marriage must not go on.

sentences.context: This ought not to be written in ink but in a golden splash
sentences.simple: This should not be written in ink but in a splash of gold.
sentences.grammar: 'ought not to be written' is a passive with 'ought to' (a should-not idea); 'not in ink but in...' sets two things against each other.

sentences.context: thus it will go on, so long as children are gay and innocent
sentences.simple: And so it will go on, as long as children are gay and innocent and heartless.
sentences.grammar: 'so long as' means 'as long as'; it joins the future 'will go on' to a condition in the present, 'are'.
